derivation: Intersected the module maps in references/<name>/workflow.md across the three systems that are actually request routers (litellm, portkey-gateway, gaie). A stage is 'shared' only when all three have a distinct piece of code doing it; routellm and llmrouterbench are offline model-choosers with no fleet, so they contribute only to the selection stage and are listed as domain_specific. The shipped task harness (task-evaluator) is the clock, the fleet and the books, not a router, so its modules are recorded separately as the contract the skeleton plugs into. This is a reference for the coding agent, not a prescription: a single-file policy that keeps these concerns separable is a legitimate realisation of it.

shared.label: Normalise the arriving request and resolve the policy that applies to it: the model it names, the set it may be substituted within, its deadline, and its declared token cost. litellm resolves a model group, portkey parses a per-request config header, gaie looks up a workload objective.
List the (provider, model) pairs that could legally serve this request at all. Structural, not situational: it answers 'who stocks this', not 'who has room'.

Remove candidates that must not be used right now: no quota headroom, known unavailable, over budget. A hard yes/no stage, kept separate from preference. All three systems fail this stage's empty result into the overload path rather than into placement.
Order the surviving candidates by preference: price, expected time to answer, remaining headroom, locality. Soft, graded, and the one stage that is explicitly pluggable in all three systems.

Decide, when the eligible set is empty, whether to wait for capacity or refuse. litellm refuses immediately unless a priority was supplied, gaie queues with a per-workload bound, portkey never queues at all. This is the stage the three systems disagree on most.
Issue the attempt and classify what came back: served, refused for quota, refused for unavailability, failed. The classification, not the error text, is what the next stage acts on.

Given a classified failure, decide what happens next and when: divert to another candidate, wait a bounded interval and retry, or give up. litellm and portkey both divert before waiting; gaie does neither.

Whatever the policy remembers between requests, with an explicit bound on each accumulator: quota counters, unavailability, per-request attempt counts, learned statistics. portkey deliberately holds none; litellm and gaie both hold several and cap them.
What the router makes visible about the decision and about its own failures. All three emit the chosen target and the attempt history; none of them lets it affect the outcome.

litellm.label: Per-provider, per-deployment and per-tag spend accumulated after each call, used to filter candidates before the next one
An indirection from a caller-facing model name to a list of concrete deployments
An opt-in ordered wait set for callers who supplied a priority, polled until the router timeout

portkey-gateway.label: A per-request nested policy tree where every strategy is a node in one recursive walk
Before- and after-request content checks that can deny a request or consume the retry budget
An optional process-wide store of previous answers, keyed by request content

gaie.label: One bounded queue per (caller, priority) pair, with a swappable policy deciding whose turn it is
A live per-target utilisation estimate that drives both refusal and the dispatch ceiling
A registry of named filters, scorers and pickers assembled into profiles at load time
A per-target staleness clock that decides whether the router's picture of a target may still be acted on

routellm.label: A per-request estimate of how well each candidate model would answer, learned offline
An offline step that turns a target share of expensive traffic into the scalar the online path compares against

llmrouterbench.label: A frozen (request x model) matrix of measured quality and measured dollars, replayed to score a policy without serving anything
A train/test boundary drawn per request rather than per row, so no model's row for a held-out request is ever seen in fitting

task-evaluator.label: The harness owns simulated time and re-invokes the policy on arrival, on wake-up and on completion
A read-only, by-value snapshot of every provider's catalogue, in-flight count, remaining request and token headroom, and outage end time
The harness's own private ledger: quality from the model actually served, dollars from a private price table, the deadline measured from arrival
The correctness oracle: illegal refusal, illegal substitution, request lost, completed twice, lost to an announced outage, request mutated, policy livelocked
